form: Modern 十 + 具; seal form 匕 目 乚 八
formNote: The Shuowen: 真，僊人變形而登天也 — “an immortal changing form and rising to Heaven”, analysing the seal form as 匕 (transformation), 目 (eye), 乚 (hidden) and 八 (the carriage). The modern split ⿱十具 is visual only.
summary: True, genuine: the real thing as against the counterfeit. Daoists spoke of the 真人, the true person; Buddhist translators wrote 真如 for suchness and 真言 for mantra; the Shingon school in Japan takes its name from it.
placement: On the left of the band, above 如 and across the axis from 實, so that 真 reaches 如, 實 and 言 alike: 真如, 真實, 真言. (Placement is a design choice, not a claim.)

oc.note: † Baracus, from general knowledge; not yet checked against B–S 2014.

satellites.title: An Immortal Rising to Heaven
satellites.evidence: The Shuowen explains 真 as 僊人變形而登天也, “an immortal changing form and rising to Heaven”. In the Han dictionary the true is first the transfigured: what is real is what has become fully itself.
satellites.caveat: A Han, Daoist-coloured explanation of the seal form. Modern palaeographers read the early graph differently, and the second sentence is a gloss on the Shuowen, not a claim about the graph’s origin.

satellites.title: The True Person of Old
satellites.evidence: Zhuangzi ch. 6: 古之真人，其寢不夢，其覺無憂 — “the true person of old slept without dreams and woke without cares.” 真 here is not a property of statements but of a way of being.

satellites.title: Truth as the Unhidden
satellites.evidence: Greek ἀλήθεια, “truth”, is built from a-, “not”, and the root of λήθη, “forgetting, concealment”: the true is what is not hidden. 真 has no such shape, but both words answer the same question: what is the case when nothing is covered over.
satellites.caveat: An analogy, not a translation: no text renders one by the other. The reading “unconcealment” owes much to Heidegger, and philologists dispute how much of the etymology Greek speakers heard.
